lead: Hand-written grammars carry baggage: nullable variables, unit chains, unreachable symbols. All legal, none helpful. Simplifying a context-free grammar removes this baggage and keeps the language unchanged. Parsers and normal-form constructions want the short version, so clean-up runs first. Three jobs: ε-rules, unit rules, useless symbols — in that order.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for productions and derivations, and 3.2 for the meaning of ⇒*.

blocks.text: A variable A is nullable if A ⇒* ε: some derivation from A ends in the empty string ε, the string of length 0.
Find the nullable set by repeating two rules. If A → ε, A is nullable. If A → X₁X₂…Xₖ and every Xᵢ is nullable, A is nullable, because each Xᵢ can be erased.

items: Compute the nullable set by these two rules.
For every rule A → α, add a copy for each non-empty way of erasing nullable symbols from α.
If ε ∈ L(G) and S appears on no right side, add S → ε. If S appears on a right side, add a new start S₀, add S₀ → S and S₀ → ε, make S₀ the start, and do not add S → ε.

blocks.text: A → α  ⇒  add A → α′ for every non-empty α′ got by erasing nullable symbols from α
blocks.where: A is a variable, α is a string of variables and terminals, α′ is non-empty and is α with some nullable symbols removed.

blocks.text: A derivation that used A ⇒ ε can use the shorter right side instead. The ε-step disappears; the language does not.
A unit production is A → B with B a single variable. It swaps one variable for another and produces no terminal, so it never helps form the final string.
Call (A, B) a unit pair if A ⇒* B using only unit rules. Every variable pairs with itself: (A, A).

items: List all unit rules; put (A, A) for every variable A.
For each unit rule A → B, add (A, B).
Close the set: if (A, B) and (B, C) are pairs, add (A, C). Repeat.
For each pair (A, B), add A → α for every non-unit rule B → α.

blocks.text: A chain of unit steps collapses to one step. The grammar has no unit rules and the same language.

sections.h3: Useless symbols, and why this goes last

blocks.text: A symbol is generating if it derives some terminal string: A ⇒* w with w in Σ*. It is reachable if it appears in some derivation from S. It is useful only if both. Otherwise it can never appear in a finished terminal derivation.

items: Mark every terminal generating. Mark A generating if some rule A → α has all symbols of α generating. Repeat.
Delete every rule that mentions a non-generating symbol.
Mark S reachable. If A is marked and A → α, mark every symbol of α. Repeat.
Delete every rule that mentions an unreachable symbol.

blocks.text: Order matters. Removing ε-rules and unit rules can leave variables with no rules or no path from S. Those passes create useless symbols, so clear useless symbols last.

Theorem. For every context-free grammar G with L(G) nonempty, there is a grammar G′ with no ε-rules except possibly S → ε, no unit rules, and no useless symbols, with L(G′) = L(G). If L(G) is empty, handle that language separately.

figure.caption: Epsilon rules first, unit rules second, useless symbols last. The language leaving the end is the one that entered.

spec.title: Clean-up order
spec.aria: The clean-up pipeline: epsilon rules first, then unit rules, then useless symbols, and the language does not change.

examples.question:
Simplify the grammar G below completely. Show the nullable set, the ε-rule removal, the unit pairs, and the useless-symbol removal.
S → AB | a
A → aA | ε
B → bB | b
C → cC | c
D → aDb
steps: Nullable set. A → ε makes A nullable. S → AB needs B nullable too; it is not. Nullable = {A}.
Add erased versions. S → AB gives S → B. A → aA gives A → a. No other rule contains a nullable symbol.
Delete ε-rules. Delete A → ε. ε ∉ L(G), so no S → ε. Now: S → AB | B | a; A → aA | a; B → bB | b; C → cC | c; D → aDb.
Unit pairs. Only unit rule is S → B. Pairs: (S,S), (A,A), (B,B), (C,C), (D,D), (S,B).
Copy and delete. From (S,B), copy B's non-unit rules: S → bB, S → b. Delete S → B. Now: S → AB | a | bB | b; A → aA | a; B → bB | b; C → cC | c; D → aDb.
Generating. Terminals a, b, c generate. A generates via A → a; B via B → b; S via S → a; C via C → c. D → aDb contains D, so D is non-generating. Delete D.
Reachable. From S: S → AB reaches A and B. A → aA reaches A; B → bB reaches B. C is never reached. Delete C.
Final. S → AB | a | bB | b; A → aA | a; B → bB | b. It has 8 productions, no ε-rules, no unit rules, no useless symbols.
examples.answer: Final grammar: S → AB | a | bB | b, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. It generates L(G) and has 8 productions, 0 nullable variables and 0 non-reflexive unit pairs.
examples.check:
final = {'S': ['AB', 'a', 'bB', 'b'], 'A': ['aA', 'a'], 'B': ['bB', 'b']}
print(len([1 for rs in final.values() for r in rs if r == 'eps']), len([1 for rs in final.values() for r in rs if len(r) == 1 and r.isupper()]), sum(map(len, final.values())))

traps: Deleting useless symbols first. Epsilon and unit removal create some unreachable and non-generating symbols; clear useless last.
Deleting S → ε when ε ∈ L(G). Keep one ε-rule, but if S appears on a right side move it to the new start: S₀ → ε, not S → ε.
Forgetting reflexive unit pairs (A, A). They add nothing new but the closure needs them.
Adding erased versions for empty results. A → ε is handled by deletion, not re-added.
Confusing generating with reachable. D → aDb is reachable but non-generating; C is generating but unreachable.

quiz.q: Define a nullable variable, a unit production and a useless symbol.
quiz.a: A is nullable if A ⇒* ε. A unit production is A → B with B a single variable. A symbol is useless if it is not both generating and reachable from S.
ε-rule and unit-rule removal can strip a variable of all rules or cut its path from S. Those passes create useless symbols, so a final pass catches all.

quiz.q: When ε ∈ L(G), where does the ε-rule go if S appears on a right side?
quiz.a: Add a new start S₀, add S₀ → S and S₀ → ε, make S₀ the start, and delete S → ε. Keeping S → ε would leave an ε-rule on a non-start variable.

quiz.q: Grammar: S → AB, A → aA | ε, B → b | ε. Find the nullable set and write the grammar after ε-elimination (ε ∈ L).
quiz.a: A and B are nullable; then S is nullable. Erased: S → A, S → B, A → a. Keep S → ε. Grammar: S → AB | A | B | ε; A → aA | a; B → b.

quiz.q: Grammar: S → A | B, A → aA | a, B → bB | b. Remove unit rules.
quiz.a: Pairs: (S,S), (A,A), (B,B), (S,A), (S,B). Add S → aA | a and S → bB | b. Delete S → A and S → B. Result: S → aA | a | bB | b; A → aA | a; B → bB | b.

quiz.q: A student removes unreachable symbols before ε-rules and loses strings. Explain.
quiz.a: At that stage some variables look reachable only through rules that ε-removal will change. Deciding reachability on the old rule set can delete live rules. Run ε, then units, then useless.

quiz.q: A grammar has no ε-rules and no unit rules but still has a non-generating variable. Can it still have useless symbols, and how do you find them?
quiz.a: Yes. Neither pass guarantees usefulness. Run the generating fixed point, delete rules touching non-generating symbols, then the reachability fixed point from S, and delete rules touching unreachable symbols.

beyond: Not for the exam. Compiler front ends run this clean-up plus left-recursion removal and left factoring before parser tables, because a smaller grammar means a smaller automaton. Parser generators warn about useless and unreachable rules. Next: left recursion elimination, left factoring, and LL(1) table construction.
